paragraphs.heading: What the law says
paragraphs.text: Faraday's law of induction explains how a changing magnetic field can drive an electric current in a circuit. This effect, called electromagnetic induction, is the basic working principle of transformers, inductors, and many motors, generators and solenoids. In its usual form, the flux rule, it says the electromotive force (emf) around a closed circuit equals the negative of how fast the magnetic flux through that circuit is changing. You can picture magnetic flux as a count of how many field lines cross the loop. The rule holds for any thin-wire circuit, whether the flux changes because the field varies, the circuit moves, or its shape is bent.

paragraphs.heading: The question before Faraday
paragraphs.text: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted showed that an electric current makes a magnetic field, by turning a compass needle with a nearby wire carrying current. Scientists then asked whether it worked the other way round. Early tests found that a magnet simply sitting near a wire loop made no current at all. In 1831 Michael Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field could do it. Joseph Henry saw similar effects in 1832, but Faraday published first.

paragraphs.heading: The iron ring
paragraphs.text: Faraday's notebook entry for August 29, 1831 records a demonstration of induction. He wound two coils of wire on opposite sides of an iron ring. When he connected one coil to a battery, a galvanometer attached to the second coil gave a brief kick. He reasoned that the changing current in the first coil made a changing magnetic field in the ring, and that this field drove a current in the second coil. In the months after, he also got brief currents by moving a bar magnet quickly into or out of a coil.

paragraphs.heading: Two versions of one law
paragraphs.text: The name Faraday's law is used for two related but distinct statements. The Maxwell–Faraday equation says a magnetic field that changes in time always comes with a circulating electric field, and it applies to the fields even when no circuit is there. The flux rule, also called the Faraday–Lenz law, ties the emf around a closed conducting loop to how fast the flux through it changes, and it can be derived from the first statement for a closed circuit. The direction comes from Lenz's law: the induced current flows so that its own magnetic field opposes the change in flux.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to make an emf
paragraphs.text: The flux rule covers two mechanisms. In transformer emf, a changing magnetic field creates an electric field, and that field pushes current around the loop. In motional emf, the loop itself travels through a magnetic field, and the magnetic part of the Lorentz force acts on the charges in the wire. The current depends only on relative motion, yet the two explanations differed, which posed a puzzle. Special relativity treats the difference as depending on the observer: a magnetic force in one frame can appear as an induced electric field in another.

paragraphs.heading: From idea to equation
paragraphs.text: Faraday explained induction with lines of force, but his ideas met doubt because they were not written as mathematics. Franz Ernst Neumann set the laws of induction in mathematical form in 1845. James Clerk Maxwell then built Faraday's insights into his wider electromagnetic theory in the early 1860s. The form found among Maxwell's equations today is Oliver Heaviside's version from the 1890s.
